opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few different mechanisms, and they work on different timescales.

The most immediate one is in-context learning. When the model is working on a task, everything it has seen so far is in the context window: the instructions, what it has tried, what failed, the error messages. A good model should already use that well. It should notice when an approach isn't working and change course rather than repeating the same mistake. Models are surprisingly good at this, and it's very sample-efficient, because you're relying on all the general knowledge from pre-training to read each new piece of evidence correctly.

The limitation is that context is finite and somewhat fragile. On a long project, say days or weeks of work, you can't keep everything in the window. So the next layer is some kind of explicit memory or note-taking. The model writes down what it has learned about the codebase or the problem, the conventions, the dead ends, and pulls that back in later. That's roughly what a human does with a lab notebook or a design doc. It's crude, but it works reasonably well and it's easy to inspect.

The more interesting open question is whether you also want some form of weight updates during the task, a kind of online fine-tuning where the model consolidates what it learned into its parameters. Humans do something like that. You don't just keep notes; after a few weeks on a project, the knowledge becomes intuitive and you stop looking things up. I think something analogous will be important for models to work on long-horizon tasks, but it's tricky. You have to avoid overfitting to noisy feedback, avoid forgetting general capabilities, and decide what's actually worth consolidating versus what was a one-off detail.

So my guess is you end up with a hierarchy: in-context learning for the moment-to-moment stuff, some kind of retrievable memory for medium-term facts, and eventually some slower consolidation into the weights. It's a bit like the different memory systems in the brain. Getting those layers to work together smoothly, so the model actually gets better over the course of a project instead of just accumulating a long transcript, is one of the more important things to figure out for making agents useful on real, extended work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the big open problems right now. When you look at how a person learns to do a job, most of the learning doesn't happen before they start. They come in with some general background, and then over the first few weeks or months they pick up all the specifics: how this particular codebase is organized, what the team cares about, which approaches tend to work and which don't. And that learning compounds. By the end of a year they're much more effective than on day one, even though their underlying intelligence hasn't changed.

Right now, models mostly don't do that. You get a model, it has a fixed set of weights, and every time you start a new session it's basically day one again. We've papered over that somewhat with long context and with retrieval, where you stuff relevant history back into the prompt, and that does help. But it's a pretty crude form of learning. It's more like carrying around a notebook than actually internalizing something.

So I think the thing we want is some notion of continual learning, where the model is actually updating as it goes through a task. There are a few ways you could imagine getting there. One is just making in-context learning really good, so the model can take a long trajectory of its own attempts, see what worked and what didn't, and adjust its behavior within that context. You can train for that explicitly, where you reward the model not just for getting the right answer but for improving across a sequence of attempts. That's sort of a meta-learning setup.

Another approach is to actually update weights during deployment, do some kind of fine-tuning on the experience the model accumulates. That's harder, because you run into all the classic problems: catastrophic forgetting, instability, and the question of what signal you're even learning from. If you're just doing self-supervised learning on your own outputs, it's not obvious you get better rather than just more confident.

I think the key ingredient in either case is having a good signal about what went well. When a person learns on the job, they're getting feedback constantly, from their manager, from whether the code compiled, from whether the customer was happy. A model carrying out a long project needs something analogous. Some of that can come from the environment, like tests passing, and some has to come from the model's own judgment about whether it's making progress. And training models to have good calibrated judgment about their own progress is itself a big piece of the puzzle.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of what fast learning looks like in practice is just being good at noticing. Noticing when you've tried the same thing three times and it didn't work. Noticing that the user keeps correcting you in the same way. Current models are often surprisingly bad at that, they'll just keep going. So before you even get to fancy weight updates, there's a lot to gain from making the model reflective about its own trajectory, and that's something you can get at with pretty standard RL if you set up the environments right.

astra-6.text:
I think you want it to learn at a couple of different timescales. While it’s working on a task, it should be keeping track of what it’s tried, what worked, and which assumptions turned out to be wrong. You can do a lot of that in context, without changing the model’s weights. If it spends an hour debugging something, you don’t want it to come back the next day and make exactly the same mistakes.

Then there’s the question of how you turn that experience into something more general. Can it learn a technique on one project and use it on the next project, where the details are different? That’s where you’d want some kind of training or consolidation, rather than just accumulating a longer and longer record of everything it did.

The tricky part is deciding what to learn from. During a project, you get a lot of feedback, but it’s often ambiguous. Something failed—was the approach wrong, or did you just implement it incorrectly? So I’d want the model to test its hypotheses and get reliable feedback as it goes. Fast learning isn’t just updating quickly; it’s figuring out which updates are actually justified.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that it should be able to learn from what happens during the task, instead of treating every step as a fresh problem. If it tries something and it doesn’t work, it should update its understanding of the situation and use that information on the next attempt.

You can do a lot of that in context. Suppose the model is working in a codebase. It discovers how to run the tests, which parts of the code are relevant, and what approaches have already failed. It should maintain that understanding as it works, so it doesn’t have to rediscover everything each time.

Then there’s a separate question of what should go into the weights. You’d like the model to retain lessons that generalize across projects, but you probably don’t want to update its weights on every observation. Some observations are misleading, and some are only relevant to the particular task.

So I’d think about it as having a fast learning process within the task, with feedback and some persistent memory, and a slower process that turns those experiences into more general skills. The interesting challenge is getting the model to recognize what it has actually learned and when that lesson applies.
